c.tagline: Dai temples, elephant-crossed jungles, and Mekong sunsets in China's tropical southern frontier.
langs: Hani, Jinuo, Bulang, and other minority languages

card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside international-brand hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay are used for nearly everything — set up mobile payment before arrival

taxi.fareNote: Meters are standard in town, but drivers to outlying villages or the botanical garden usually quote a flat round-trip fare

emergency.medical: 120 (ambulance); Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture People's Hospital in Jinghong
emergency.note: Heat exhaustion and river-current incidents are the most common tourist emergencies; English support is limited outside major hotels

religion: Han Chinese majority nonreligious or Mahayana Buddhist/Taoist
walk: Jinghong's riverside core and night-market streets are pleasant on foot, but most major sights — the botanical garden, elephant valley, Dai villages — require a car, bus, or Didi ride out of town

safety.safety: Very safe, relaxed resort-town atmosphere popular with solo Chinese travelers
safety.crime: Low — biggest risks are heat/sun exposure, river currents, and tourist-market overcharging

hood_landmark.Jinghong City Center: Mekong River promenade and Peacock Lake
hood_landmark.Gaozhuang Night Market: Gaozhuang International Trade City night market

hood_desc: The Mekong-side core of wide boulevards and palm trees, with the riverside promenade, prefecture museum, and Peacock Lake nearby.
Home to Manting Park's royal Dai gardens and Buddhist temples, a green, templed pocket just east of downtown.
Jinghong's after-dark hub of skewer stalls, fruit vendors, and bars, busiest after sunset when the heat breaks.
A cluster of traditional Dai stilt-house villages and the Dai Minority Garden theme park, downstream along the Mekong.
Home to the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, a riverbend peninsula of rainforest about an hour from the city.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water, as locals do.

transit.sys: City buses plus long-distance minibuses to Dai villages and Menglun
transit.note: No metro; Didi ride-hailing covers the city well, but rural villages and gardens need buses or a hired driver

transport.air: Xishuangbanna Gasa International Airport (JHG), ~6 km from downtown Jinghong, with flights to Kunming, other major Chinese cities, and a handful of Southeast Asia routes
transport.train: Xishuangbanna (Jinghong) railway station on the China–Laos Railway — direct high-speed service to Kunming (~3.5 hrs) and onward to Vientiane, Laos
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect Jinghong to Kunming (~8-10 hrs by road) and cross-border routes toward Laos and Myanmar
transport.ferry: Seasonal Mekong River cargo/passenger boats run toward Laos, though scheduled tourist ferry service is limited
transport.car: Self-driving or a hired driver is useful for reaching Dai villages, tea mountains, and the botanical garden, which are spread across the prefecture

airport.name: Xishuangbanna Gasa International Airport
airport.transport: Taxi ~$5-8 metered fare into town; airport shuttle bus to the city center also available

net.m: Good 4G/5G in Jinghong city; coverage thins out in remote Dai villages and tea-mountain areas
net.w: Free wifi at hotels and cafes in the city center
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.fwn: VPN required for Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and most Western apps
net.ap: SIM/eSIM is easiest to buy in Kunming before flying or training in; Jinghong airport has a China Mobile counter

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture and can even confuse staff
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; a service charge is occasionally added automatically at upscale hotel restaurants

food.name: Lemongrass-grilled fish
food.desc: Whole tilapia split flat, stuffed with lemongrass, coriander and chilli, clamped in bamboo and grilled over coals - the defining Dai dish.

places.name: Gaozhuang Xishuangjing Night Market
places.area: Gaozhuang, east bank of the Mekong
places.note: Jinghong's biggest night market; rows of coal grills firing from about 5pm.

places.name: Jiangbian (riverside) Night Market
places.note: Lantern-lit riverside stalls, roughly 6pm to midnight; grilled fish everywhere.

places.name: Manting Road Dai restaurants
places.note: Sit-down Dai restaurants near the park doing full grilled-fish meals.

food.name: Pineapple rice
food.desc: Sticky rice steamed with pineapple flesh inside a hollowed-out pineapple, sometimes with raisins and coconut; sweet, sticky and shareable.

places.name: Gaozhuang Xishuangjing Night Market
places.note: Stalls sell whole stuffed pineapples ready to eat with a spoon.

places.name: Manting Road Dai restaurants
places.note: Restaurant versions arrive hot with the pineapple used as the bowl.

places.name: Xingguang (Starlight) Night Market
places.note: Smaller riverside market with Dai snacks and tropical fruit.

food.name: Sour bamboo shoot soup with fish
food.desc: Fermented bamboo shoots simmered with river fish, tomato, lemongrass and chilli into a sharp, sour broth - the Dai kitchen's everyday soup.

places.name: Manting Road Dai restaurants
places.note: Family-run Dai kitchens where suan sun yu is a menu staple.

places.name: Gaozhuang Xishuangjing Night Market
places.note: Sit-down stalls inside the market serve claypot sour bamboo soups.

places.name: Jinghong farmers markets
places.note: Morning markets sell the fermented bamboo and herbs behind the dish.

food.name: Dai grilled chicken
food.desc: Chicken flattened, marinated with lemongrass and Sichuan-style spice, then charcoal-grilled and served with a sour-chilli dipping powder.

places.name: Gaozhuang Xishuangjing Night Market
places.note: Whole and half birds grilled to order; go 7pm to 9pm for the best choice.

places.name: Jiangbian (riverside) Night Market
places.note: Riverside grills doing chicken alongside pork belly and fish.

places.name: Manting Road Dai restaurants
places.note: Restaurant versions come with sticky rice and herb salads.

food.name: Dai herb and lemon salads
food.desc: Raw beef or shredded chicken tossed with lime, wild herbs, chilli and garlic; the bitter niu sapie version uses cattle bile for a serious local challenge.

places.name: Manting Road Dai restaurants
places.note: Best place to try lemon beef salad and the bolder Dai bitter dishes.

places.name: Gaozhuang Xishuangjing Night Market
places.note: Salad stalls mix to order; point at the herbs you want included.

places.name: Jiangbian (riverside) Night Market
places.note: Cold-dish counters serve herb salads as a foil to the grills.

food.name: Bamboo-tube sticky rice
food.desc: Glutinous rice packed with coconut milk into a green bamboo tube and roasted until the rice takes on the bamboo's fragrance; split open to eat.

places.name: Gaozhuang Xishuangjing Night Market
places.note: Bamboo tubes roasted over coals at the entrance stalls; cheap snack.

places.name: Jiangbian (riverside) Night Market
places.note: Sold alongside grilled fish as the standard starch to share.

places.name: Manting Park food stalls
places.note: Stalls around the park sell bamboo rice and coconut jelly to visitors.

food.name: Pu-erh tea
food.desc: Xishuangbanna is the historic home of pu-erh; the ancient tea forests of Menghai and Yiwu supply both raw sheng and aged shu cakes.

places.name: Gaozhuang Xishuangjing tea houses
places.note: Numerous tea shops offer free tastings of sheng and shu pu-erh.

places.name: Manting Road tea shops
places.note: Older tea street where local dealers sell by the cake; ask to taste first.

places.name: Jinghong tea wholesale market
places.note: Bulk market where pu-erh from surrounding mountains is traded.

food.name: Lao-style iced coffee
food.desc: Thick, sweet iced coffee with condensed milk, a legacy of Xishuangbanna's Mekong ties with Laos and Thailand; local Yunnan beans are also strong.

places.name: Gaozhuang Xishuangjing Night Market
places.note: Coffee stalls pour Lao-style iced coffee among the food carts.

places.name: Xingguang (Starlight) Night Market
places.note: Riverside stalls selling iced coffee, coconut and fruit shakes.

places.name: Manting Road cafes
places.note: Small cafes using Yunnan-grown beans; good escape from the heat.

landmarks: Mengle Grand Buddha Temple (Wat Mengle)
Xishuangbanna's grandest Theravada temple climbs a hillside in golden tiers to a towering standing Buddha overlooking Jinghong's palm-lined streets.
Gaozhuang Xishuangjing Starlight Night Market
A riotous riverside night bazaar of golden pagodas, Dai barbecue stalls, tropical fruit juices and crafts, glittering like a slice of Southeast Asia.
Manting Park
Once the Dai kings' royal garden, this 1,300-year-old park blends peacocks, white pagodas, banyan trees and nightly water-splashing festival performances.
Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden
China's largest botanical garden sprawls across a Mekong-tributary island at Menglun, showcasing 13,000 plant species from rainforest giants to dancing grass.
Wild Elephant Valley
A rainforest reserve north of the city where wild Asian elephants roam beneath canopy walkways and cable cars in China's last elephant habitat.
Dai Ethnic Garden (Ganlanba)
Five traditional stilt-house villages within a living cultural park at Menghan, famous for daily water-splashing celebrations and authentic Dai hospitality.
Manfeilong Pagodas (Bamboo Shoot Pagoda)
A cluster of whitewashed stupas from 1204 rising like bamboo shoots above Damenglong village, the finest example of Dai Buddhist architecture.
Jingzhen Octagonal Pavilion
An exquisite 1701 Buddhist pavilion in Menghai county, its ten-sided, multi-tiered roof of tiny tiles said to imitate the Buddha's bamboo hat.
Xishuangbanna Primeval Forest Park
Rainforest trails, peacock flight displays and aerial walkways just outside Jinghong offer the easiest immersion in Banna's steamy tropical jungle.
Lancang (Mekong) Riverfront and Night Cruise
Sunset cruises and promenade strolls along the Mekong reveal Jinghong's skyline of gilded roofs as long-haul cargo boats set off toward Thailand.

intl.to: Boten, Luang Namtha, Luang Prabang & Vientiane (Laos)
intl.op: China Railway / Laos-China Railway Company (Kunming-Vientiane through service D87/D88)

train.note: Jinghong is served by Xishuangbanna station on the Yuxi-Mohan (China-Laos) railway, which opened in December 2021 and put Kunming about 3 hours away - a transformation on the old overnight bus. The same line carries the Kunming-Vientiane international through train (D87/D88) via the border at Mohan/Boten, so cross-border travel is possible from here, but international seats are released only a few days ahead, are sold through 12306 and station counters rather than freely online, and are far scarcer than domestic ones - check the current timetable before assuming your train stops here. You must have a Laos e-visa in advance because visa on arrival is not issued at Boten, and everyone leaves the train with their luggage for passport checks on both sides of the border.

intl.to: Luang Namtha, Oudomxay & Luang Prabang (Laos) - via the Mohan/Boten crossing
intl.op: cross-border sleeper coaches from Jinghong bus station, tickets at the counter or through 12Go

bus.note: Jinghong's bus stations sit close to the centre and remain useful even now the railway has opened. More than a dozen daily sleeper buses run from Kunming between 09:00 and 22:00 for ¥150-260, taking roughly 8 hours over rough terrain, and from the Lao border town of Mohan a direct bus takes about 3 hours, though many travellers change at Mengla instead. Reaching the Yuanyang terraces means connecting through Jianshui or Luchun, a journey of around 12 hours. Cross-border coaches need your Laos visa arranged before you board.

ferry.note: Jinghong sits on the Lancang (Mekong) and its port still handles Chinese cargo boats heading downstream, but the scheduled passenger sailings that once ran to Chiang Saen in Thailand no longer operate, so there is no ferry you can simply buy a ticket for. Local sightseeing cruises on the river within Xishuangbanna are the only boats open to visitors.

half.name: Mandian Waterfalls
half.blurb: A jungle waterfall reached by a short hike through dense forest, with a pool beneath a 20-meter cascade for swimming.

half.name: Menghai (Aini Village & Pu'er Tea)
half.blurb: Pu'er tea plantations and Hani ethnic villages around Menghai county, reachable by a short drive and connection from Jinghong.

half.name: Jinuo Ethnic Village
half.blurb: A settlement of the Jinuo ethnic minority with traditional stilt houses and cultural performances outside Jinghong.
